screens.title: Setting Up Your Ethereum Development Environment with Hardhat
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build a reliable development environment around Hardhat so you can write, compile, and test smart contracts rapidly. Hardhat is a JavaScript-based toolkit that gives you a local in-memory blockchain, compilation and testing tools, and a plugin system you can extend. You will see why Node. js and npm are prerequisites, how to initialize a project with the Hardhat CLI, and how the generated files—contracts, scripts, tests, and hardhat. config. js—fit together. We'll also demonstrate compiling a Solidity contract to reveal the artifacts: the ABI and bytecode that client code uses to interact with deployed contracts. Finally, you'll run the Hardhat Network locally to inspect pre-funded test accounts and iterate without spending real Ether. A common misconception is that this setup is optional or that testnets are always necessary; in reality, a reproducible local network accelerates development and isolates problems before you use a public testnet. By the end of this chapter you will be able to initialize a project, resolve basic configuration mismatches, and start a local node for fast feedback. Consider how instant transactions and deterministic accounts will change your debugging flow.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to set up a full Hardhat project, understand the structure that Hardhat generates, compile Solidity contracts and read the resulting artifacts, and run a local Hardhat Network for fast testing. First, you'll install Node. js and Hardhat and initialize a Node project. Then you'll examine the folders Hardhat creates—contracts, scripts, tests—and learn how hardhat. config. js controls the compiler and networks. You will compile a sample contract and inspect the ABI and bytecode so you see exactly how human-readable code maps to deployable artifacts. Finally, you will start the Hardhat Network and use the provided pre-funded accounts for deploying and testing without spending real Ether. Each objective includes a short practical milestone so you can verify competency: initialize a project, adjust a compiler version, compile a contract without errors, and run the local node. Along the way we will discuss common mistakes like version mismatches and missing dependencies and how to resolve them quickly.

screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide describes the practical checks you'll do as you follow the hands-on activity. screens.title: What is Hardhat?
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat is a developer-focused framework that automates common tasks when building smart contracts and decentralized applications. At its core it provides compilation tools, a testing framework, and an in-memory local blockchain called Hardhat Network. Think of Hardhat as the glue that ties your Solidity code, JavaScript tooling, and local test blockchain together. One concrete example: you write a contract in Solidity, run the compiler through Hardhat, and immediately receive artifacts—an ABI and bytecode—that your deployment scripts and front end use. A common misconception is that Hardhat is only a testing tool; while testing is a strong part, Hardhat also manages compilation, plugins, network configurations, and scriptable deployments. Another contrast is with running a public testnet: Hardhat Network is ephemeral and instant, letting you run thousands of tests quickly and reset state between runs, whereas public testnets involve latency and cost. Key takeaway: Hardhat streamlines the development loop so you can iterate quickly and catch errors early. Ask yourself: how would instant local transactions speed up your debugging compared with waiting for real block confirmations? What is Hardhat? means hardhat is a modular javascript-based environment that compiles, tests, and runs a local ethereum node to speed development cycles.. In practical terms, a development environment for compiling, deploying, testing, and debugging ethereum software. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is Hardhat?
Definition
Hardhat is a development environment for compiling, deploying, testing, and debugging smart contracts. It combines a compiler interface, task runner, plugin system, and a local blockchain.
Feature: built-in local blockchain for fast iteration
Feature: plugin ecosystem and ethers.js integration
Feature: deterministic accounts and easy scripting
Analogy
Hardhat is like a local test lab: you write code, run experiments instantly, and examine results without touching the public network.
Concrete example
Write a simple contract, run npx hardhat compile, and use the produced ABI to call functions from a script—no Ether required.
Key Takeaway

Hardhat accelerates iteration by combining compilation, local chain simulation, and test automation in one tool.

screens.title: Prerequisites and Installation
screens.narratorSegment: Before you use Hardhat you must have Node. js and npm installed because Hardhat runs on the Node runtime and uses npm to manage packages. A practical way to manage versions is a version manager, but the essential steps are straightforward. Create a new project folder, run npm init -y to generate package. json, then add Hardhat as a development dependency with npm install --save-dev hardhat. A concrete example: from an empty folder run the sequence and you will see package. json updated with a devDependency entry for hardhat and a node_modules directory created. A common mistake is skipping npm install before running npx hardhat init—npx may still run, but local dependencies will be missing for other scripts. Another pitfall is using an unsupported Node version; if you encounter cryptic build errors, confirm your Node version. The takeaway: ensure Node and npm are ready, initialize package. json, and install Hardhat locally. This gives you predictable tooling behavior across machines and makes the project reproducible. Prerequisites and Installation means node and npm must be available, package.json initialized, and hardhat installed as a devdependency for predictable project behavior.. In practical terms, install node.js, use npm, and add hardhat to your project. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Prerequisites & Install
Installation steps
Follow these shell commands to create a reproducible project.
mkdir my-first-hardhat-project
cd my-first-hardhat-project
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev hardhat
  • npm init creates package.json that records devDependencies.
  • Installing hardhat locally keeps the project self-contained.
  • Use npx to run Hardhat commands from the local node_modules folder.
Concrete example
After installation, package.json will include a devDependencies entry for hardhat. You can now run npx hardhat to initialize or compile.
Common mistake: skipping npm install or using a different package manager without verifying devDependencies.
Key Takeaway

Install Hardhat locally and confirm package.json lists it under devDependencies to ensure consistent behavior.

screens.title: Initializing a Hardhat Project
screens.narratorSegment: Initializing a Hardhat project is an interactive step that scaffolds the directories and configuration you need. Run npx hardhat init and the tool will prompt you to choose a project type. For learners, selecting 'Create a basic sample project' is a convenient start because it provides a sample contract, a deployment script, and a test file you can compile and run immediately. Alternatively, choosing an empty hardhat. config. js is useful when you want full control. The initialization creates folders like contracts, scripts, and test, and writes hardhat. config. js, which centralizes compiler and network settings. A common confusion arises from npx behavior: npx runs locally installed binaries when available, otherwise it fetches packages temporarily; for reproducibility prefer local installation and explicit devDependency entries. Example result: after init you should see contracts/ with a sample Lock. sol, scripts/ with deploy scripts, and a hardhat. config. js with a solidity field. Double-check the solidity version in the config to match any pragma statements in your contracts to avoid compile-time mismatches. Initializing a Hardhat Project means npx hardhat init scaffolds a project with contracts, scripts, tests, and hardhat.config.js that you can immediately compile and test.. In practical terms, use npx hardhat init to create a minimal sample project or an empty config. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: A Simple Solidity Contract and Compilation
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through a concise Solidity example and show how Hardhat compiles it into artifacts. Consider a small contract that stores a greeting string and exposes a setter. When you run npx hardhat compile, the compiler produces a JSON artifact with the contract's ABI and bytecode in the artifacts folder. The ABI is a JSON array describing functions and events so external scripts can call the contract, and the bytecode is the machine code deployed to the EVM. A concrete example is the following contract that sets and reads a greeting. After compilation, you can open artifacts/contracts/MyContract. sol/MyContract. json and find the ABI and bytecode keys. A common misunderstanding is to treat the ABI as executable code—ABI is only a description. Key takeaway: compile to produce artifacts, then use the ABI and bytecode for deployment and interaction. A Simple Solidity Contract and Compilation means compiling with hardhat generates json artifacts containing the abi and bytecode that client code needs to interact with and deploy the contract.. In practical terms, inspect mycontract.sol and run npx hardhat compile to produce artifacts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Compile Example
Sample contract
This example demonstrates a basic contract with a constructor and a setter function. Compile it with npx hardhat compile.
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract MyContract {
  string public greeting;

  constructor(string memory _greeting) {
    greeting = _greeting;
  }

  function setGreeting(string memory _newGreeting) public {
    greeting = _newGreeting;
  }
}
Compile command
npx hardhat compile
Artifacts explained
  • ABI: JSON array describing functions and events for external interaction.
  • Bytecode: Deployable EVM machine code created by the compiler.
  • Location: artifacts/contracts/MyContract.sol/MyContract.json
Key Takeaway

Use the ABI to call contract functions and the bytecode to deploy—the artifacts bridge your source to the blockchain.

screens.title: Hardhat Network and Pre-funded Accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat Network is an in-memory blockchain optimized for development. You start it with npx hardhat node and the command prints a list of pre-funded deterministic accounts and their private keys. These accounts let you deploy and interact with contracts without spending real Ether and they make tests reproducible because the initial state is the same each run. A concrete scenario: start the node and use the first account's private key in a deployment script to send a contract to the network; transactions are processed instantly with no gas cost implications in the local environment. A frequent misconception is treating these accounts as secure—remember they exist only for development and should never be used outside a local environment. Also note the node is ephemeral: stopping and restarting resets the chain state, which is a feature for clean tests but not a replacement for persistent testnets. Key takeaway: use Hardhat Network to iterate quickly, run automated tests, and simulate multiple user accounts without real funds. Hardhat Network and Pre-funded Accounts means hardhat network provides fast, deterministic, ephemeral accounts for safe and repeatable contract testing and development.. In practical terms, start npx hardhat node to get a local blockchain with deterministic accounts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Understanding hardhat.config.js
screens.narratorSegment: The hardhat. config. js file is the central place where you tell Hardhat which Solidity compiler version to use, what networks to target, and which plugins to load. A minimal config usually includes a solidity field with a version string, for example 0.8.20 or another compatible release. This setting must be compatible with the pragma lines in your contracts; otherwise the compiler will produce a version mismatch error. You can also register named networks for deployment scripts, attach A P I keys for external services via plugins, and add compilation settings like optimizer runs. A common troubleshooting step is to open hardhat. config. js when you see compilation errors that reference the compiler: verify the solidity field matches the project contracts. Example: adjusting the solidity version to match a contract's pragma resolves many initial errors. Key takeaway: always confirm your hardhat. config. js compiler entry aligns with the pragma directives in your contracts to avoid compilation failures. Understanding hardhat.config.js means hardhat.config.js defines compiler versions, networks, and plugins; mismatches between config and contract pragma are a frequent source of errors.. In practical terms, control compilers, networks, and plugins from a single configuration file. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Local Node vs Public Testnet
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding when to use a local node versus a public testnet is important for efficient development. Hardhat Network is ideal for iteration: it is instant, free, deterministic, and ephemeral, so you can run rapid tests and reset state between runs. Public testnets simulate the mainnet environment more closely and are useful for integration testing, gas estimation, and interactions with other deployed contracts, but they have latency and may require acquiring test Ether. A practical workflow is to develop and unit-test locally with Hardhat Network, then run integration tests and final checks on a public testnet before any mainnet deployment. A common mistake is skipping public testnet validation entirely; while local tests catch many issues, they cannot replicate all external integrations. screens.title: Troubleshooting Initial Setup
screens.narratorSegment: Setup issues are common when you start a new Hardhat project, but most have straightforward resolutions. One frequent error is a compiler version mismatch where the contract's pragma and the configured compiler in hardhat. config. js are incompatible. The fix is to either change the solidity field in hardhat. config. js to a compatible version or update the pragma in your contract to match the configured compiler. Another common problem is forgetting to run npm install so the local node_modules folder is missing required packages; reinstalling dependencies resolves this. Typos in file paths or hardhat. config. js field names can also break compilation or runtime tasks; in those cases, carefully re-open the config and compare fields to the expected format. The assessment example in this chapter illustrates diagnosing a version mismatch error message and resolving it by aligning versions. Key takeaway: read error messages carefully, check package. json and hardhat. config. js for correct entries, and ensure you installed devDependencies locally before running commands. In this lesson we will build a reliable development environment around Hardhat so you can write, compile, and test smart contracts rapidly. Hardhat is a JavaScript-based toolkit that gives you a local in-memory blockchain, compilation and testing tools, and a plugin system you can extend. You will see why Node. js and npm are prerequisites, how to initialize a project with the Hardhat CLI, and how the generated files—contracts, scripts, tests, and hardhat. config. js—fit together. We'll also demonstrate compiling a Solidity contract to reveal the artifacts: the ABI and bytecode that client code uses to interact with deployed contracts. Finally, you'll run the Hardhat Network locally to inspect pre-funded test accounts and iterate without spending real Ether. A common misconception is that this setup is optional or that testnets are always necessary; in reality, a reproducible local network accelerates development and isolates problems before you use a public testnet. By the end of this chapter you will be able to initialize a project, resolve basic configuration mismatches, and start a local node for fast feedback. Consider how instant transactions and deterministic accounts will change your debugging flow.

Then you'll examine the folders Hardhat creates—contracts, scripts, tests—and learn how hardhat. config. js controls the compiler and networks. Finally, you will start the Hardhat Network and use the provided pre-funded accounts for deploying and testing without spending real Ether. Each objective includes a short practical milestone so you can verify competency: initialize a project, adjust a compiler version, compile a contract without errors, and run the local node. Along the way we will discuss common mistakes like version mismatches and missing dependencies and how to resolve them quickly.

For each step there is a simple verification: the package. json contains hardhat as a devDependency, the contracts folder contains the sample contract, compilation produces an artifacts directory with a JSON ABI file, and the node command prints pre-funded accounts and private keys. A typical misconception is believing the node must be persistent; remember the network resets each run and is intended for ephemeral fast tests.
